opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's one of the most exciting areas right now, partly because kernel writing is such a bottleneck. There just aren't that many people who can write really fast attention kernels or GEMM kernels for new hardware, and every time a new chip comes out, whether it's a new generation of Nvidia GPUs or AMD or one of the custom accelerators, there's a lag of months or even a year before the software catches up. So if models can help close that gap, the payoff is huge.

The nice thing about kernels as a domain is that you have a very clear verification signal. You can check correctness against a reference implementation, and you can measure speed. That's exactly the kind of setting where you can do a lot of reinforcement learning or search, because the reward isn't fuzzy. Compare that to writing a big software system, where it's much harder to say whether the output is good.

But the hard part is that current models haven't seen much high-quality kernel code. There's a lot of Python and JavaScript on the internet, but very little really optimized CUDA, and even less for the newest hardware features. So the models tend to write something that's correct but slow, or something that looks plausible but has subtle bugs, like race conditions or wrong memory layouts.

So I see a few pieces coming together. One is better abstractions. Things like Triton, or the DSLs people are building on top of CUTLASS, make the search space smaller and more structured, so it's easier for a model to produce something reasonable. Two is the feedback loop: let the model compile, run, profile, look at where the bottleneck is, and iterate, the way a human expert would. And three is generating data, using that loop to produce lots of verified, fast kernels that you then train on.

I don't think we're at the point where the model replaces the expert. In the near term it's more like the expert can get ten times as much done, because the model handles a lot of the boilerplate and exploration of different tiling choices and so on. But I'm pretty optimistic that within a couple of years, a good chunk of the kernels people use day to day will be at least partly written by models.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because writing kernels is honestly most of what I do, and it's painful. It's slow, it requires a ton of specialized knowledge about the hardware, and there are maybe a few hundred people in the world who can do it well. So if models can help here, that's a huge lever.

I think the path has a few pieces. The first is that the models are actually already pretty good at the easy stuff. If you ask them to write a simple elementwise kernel, or a reduction, or a straightforward Triton kernel, they'll do it, and it'll be correct and reasonably fast. Where they fall down is the hard stuff, the kind of thing that gets you from, say, 50 percent of hardware peak to 75 or 80 percent. That requires understanding things like how the memory hierarchy works on Hopper or Blackwell, how to use TMA, how to overlap the tensor core computation with memory movement, how to deal with bank conflicts in shared memory, register pressure, all of that. And a lot of that knowledge just isn't written down very much. It's in people's heads, it's in a few blog posts, it's in the CUTLASS source code. So the training data is thin.

The second piece, which I think is really the key one, is that kernel generation is a domain where you can verify. You can check correctness against a reference implementation, and you can measure speed. You just run it. So this is a natural fit for the whole reinforcement learning, test-time compute direction, where the model proposes something, you get a signal back, and it iterates. The feedback loop is tight and the reward is unambiguous, which is exactly the setting where these methods have worked best, like in math and coding. The catch is you need actual hardware in the loop, and you need to be careful about reward hacking, where the model does something like cheat on the benchmark by caching results or only handling the test shapes. We've seen that kind of thing happen.

The third thing is that I don't think the models should necessarily be writing raw CUDA or PTX. The better abstraction layer matters a lot. If you give the model something like Triton, or ThunderKittens, or the CuTe DSL, where a lot of the hardware-specific complexity is already packaged into primitives, the search space gets much smaller and the model can focus on the algorithmic decisions, like tiling strategy, pipelining depth, how to split work across warps. Humans are more productive at that level too, so it's not surprising the models are.

So my mental model is that in the near term, it's a collaboration. The model handles the first draft, the boilerplate, the exploration of a bunch of tiling configurations, and the expert handles the final 20 percent and the new hardware features that nobody has written about yet. Over time I expect that boundary moves. I'm actually fairly optimistic. I'd guess within a couple of years, for most common operators, you can get to near-expert performance largely automatically, and the human effort shifts toward the genuinely novel algorithmic ideas, which is the part I find fun anyway.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to give models a really good feedback loop. With GPU kernels, you can check whether the output is correct, and then you can measure how fast it runs. So the model can propose an implementation, run it, look at the results, and iterate.

The hard part is that correctness and performance are very different targets. You can write a kernel that computes the right answer but is much slower than an existing library. To improve it, you need to understand things like memory access, how much work you’re assigning to each thread block, and what’s limiting performance on that particular GPU. I’d want the model to have access to profiling tools, not just a timing number.

My guess is that the first useful systems will work on fairly constrained problems: a particular operation, a known set of input shapes, a particular piece of hardware. Even there, they could be valuable. There are lots of combinations of operations where writing a specialized kernel by hand takes more engineering time than you can justify. If a model can reliably handle those cases, test its work, and deliver a measurable speedup, that’s already useful. Then you can gradually expand the range of problems it can tackle.

r001.rationale: The response discusses model iteration and constrained tasks, but does not identify abundant synthetic training data generated from a small amount of expert code.

r002.rationale: It does not mention the PyTorch compiler or paired PyTorch programs and Triton kernels as training data.

r003.rationale: The response describes a model proposing, running, and refining kernels, but does not present models working alongside humans as an alternative to full automation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to give models a really good feedback loop. For GPU kernels, you can check whether the output is correct, and then you can measure how fast it runs. That gives you a concrete way to evaluate what the model produces.

The hard part is that a kernel can be correct and still be very slow. Performance depends on the hardware, the input shapes, the memory access patterns, and how you split the work across the GPU. So the model needs to do more than write code once. It needs to compile it, run it, look at the results, and iterate.

I’d start with fairly constrained tasks: here’s an operation, here are the shapes we care about, and here’s the GPU. Can you produce a correct implementation and beat a baseline? If models get good at that, you can gradually expand to fusing operations and making bigger implementation choices. You don’t need to solve every kernel to make this useful—even helping engineers explore and test more candidates could be valuable.
